group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 53-year-old man with long-standing systolic pump dysfunction from an anterior wall myocardial infarction a decade ago and compensated alcohol-related cirrhosis currently followed by hepatology every six months was brought to the emergency department by his partner after awakening at dawn acting “spacey,” misplacing the coffeepot in the refrigerator, and repeatedly asking what year it was. According to the partner, the patient had felt increasingly febrile and short of breath for three days, trying to sleep upright in a recliner because lying flat made him “drown in his chest,” and yesterday he produced several teaspoons of thick, blood-streaked sputum. He denied chest pressure, palpitations, or leg pain but complained that each breath stabbed beneath the right scapula. The patient normally manages his own medications—carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, furosemide 20 mg every morning, and lactulose 20 g as needed for constipation—and still works part-time as a mechanic, though he abandoned heavy lifting after being told his ejection fraction was in the low thirties last spring. He has no history of dialysis, nephrolithiasis, or proteinuric syndromes, has never undergone chemotherapy or radiation, and his last clinic notes list creatinine 0.9 mg/dL and normal estimated filtration. He quit cigarettes fifteen years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, drinks no alcohol since his cirrhosis diagnosis, and uses no illicit substances. He received an influenza vaccine at work in October but declined the pneumococcal booster offered by primary care. En route, emergency medical technicians placed him on a cardiac monitor but administered no oxygen, fluids, or medications so baseline values could be captured on arrival. At triage—prior to antipyretics, antibiotics, diuretics, or supplemental oxygen—his tympanic temperature registered 39.6 °C, radial pulse 114 beats per minute in a regular rhythm, automated blood pressure 129/74 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 42 breaths per minute with pronounced use of sternocleidomastoid and intercostal muscles, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuated between 88–89 % while he breathed ambient air. He sat leaning forward on the stretcher, diaphoretic, intermittently answering questions incorrectly; Glasgow Coma Scale scored 13 due to disorientation to time and place. Skin was warm with mild palmar erythema, conjunctivae anicteric, sclerae without icterus, and there was no asterixis. Jugular venous contour was 6 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, similar to recent cardiology assessments. Cardiac examination revealed a tachycardic S1 and S2 with a soft holosystolic murmur along the lower left sternal border consistent with chronic functional regurgitation, without gallops or rubs. Pulmonary exam demonstrated absent breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion over the lower half of the right posterior thorax, with bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles just above that level; the left lung had scattered late inspiratory crackles but remained resonant. Abdomen was distended to the examiner’s eye yet soft, with a smooth, palpable liver edge two centimeters below the costal margin and no shifting dullness; splenomegaly was not appreciated. Lower extremities were free of edema but displayed telangiectatic spider angiomata on the anterior thighs. Rapid capillary glucose measured 138 mg/dL. Venous and arterial blood samples drawn within ten minutes of arrival, before any intravenous flush other than small heparin locks, revealed sodium 124 mEq/L, potassium 3.8 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 28 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 37 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and hematocrit 55 %. White blood cell count was 15.4 × 10⁹/L with 87 % neutrophils, platelet count 132 × 10⁹/L, international normalized ratio 1.4, and total bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL. An arterial blood gas obtained on room air showed pH 7.55, PaCO₂ 29 mm Hg, PaO₂ 79 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, consistent with respiratory alkalosis superimposed on chronic ventilatory compromise. A portable posteroanterior and lateral chest radiograph, completed before any therapy, demonstrated a dense consolidation occupying most of the right lower lobe with a concave meniscus sign rising to the fourth posterior rib space, blunting the costophrenic sulcus and displacing the minor fissure upward, while the cardiac silhouette was enlarged but unchanged from an outpatient film three months earlier; pulmonary vasculature was cephalized yet without overt interstitial edema. Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 112 bpm with left bundle-branch block unchanged from prior. Bedside thoracic ultrasound corroborated an anechoic stripe measuring up to 3 cm over the right hemidiaphragm with dynamic air bronchograms within consolidated parenchyma. Two sets of blood cultures, expectorated sputum for Gram stain and cultures, pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigens, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were obtained while the patient remained on room air. At the time this note is recorded he has received no intravenous crystalloid, vasopressors, diuretic doses, antipyretic agents, or supplemental oxygen, and antibiotic therapy has not yet begun, ensuring that the physiological and laboratory data above reflect his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points using untreated admission findings:
- Demographics: a man's baseline score is his age → 53. No nursing-home residence → 0.
- Comorbidities: cirrhosis → 20; chronic systolic heart failure → 10. No documented malignancy, cerebrovascular disease, or chronic renal disease → 0 each.
- Examination: new disorientation → 20; RR 42/min (≥30) → 20. Systolic BP 129 mm Hg (not <90), temperature 39.6°C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 114/min (<125) → 0 each.
- Laboratory findings: BUN 37 mg/dL (≥30) → 20; sodium 124 mEq/L (<130) → 20. Arterial pH 7.55 (not <7.35), glucose 138 mg/dL (<250), and hematocrit 55% (not <30%) → 0 each. Using the measured room-air arterial PaO₂ of 79 mm Hg, the PaO₂ <60 mm Hg criterion is not met → 0, despite the discordant pulse oximetry.
- Imaging: right pleural effusion → 10.
Sum: 53 + 20 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 173.
Final answer: 173
